passages.title: The Rhyme Problem
passages.text:
Every translator of poetry eventually faces the same choice, and most of us make it badly at least once. The poem in front of you rhymes. The language you are translating into does not share its sounds. You can keep the rhyme and bend the meaning to fit it, or keep the meaning and let the rhyme go. For years I believed that the second choice was the honest one.

My reasoning seemed sound. A rhyme is an accident of a particular language: that "heart" rhymes with "part" in English says nothing about hearts. When a translator forces English rhymes onto, say, an Italian poem, the English words are chosen for their endings rather than their sense, and the poem fills with padding—adjectives that are there only because they chime, lines turned around until they sound like nothing anyone has ever said aloud. I had read enough rhymed translations of that kind to distrust the whole enterprise. So for my first book I translated a collection of short rhymed lyrics into plain, unrhymed lines, and I was proud of how closely each line followed the original.

The book was reviewed kindly and read by almost no one. That in itself did not trouble me; translated poetry is rarely read widely. What troubled me was a letter from a reader who had grown up hearing these poems sung by her grandmother. She wrote that my versions were accurate and that she did not recognize them. "You have told me what the poems say," she wrote. "You have not told me what they are like."

I resisted her point for a long time, because accepting it seemed to mean accepting the padding I disliked. But the more I reread the originals, the more I saw that their rhymes were not decoration laid over the meaning. In many of the poems, the rhyme was where the meaning happened: a word at the end of one line would be answered, two lines later, by a word that sounded like it and meant something close to its opposite, so that the ear heard agreement while the mind heard argument. My accurate versions had kept both words and lost the collision between them.

This did not convert me to rhyme at any cost. Some of the strictly rhymed translations I had distrusted really are as bad as I thought. What changed was my sense of what a translator owes the original. I had treated a poem as a set of statements that happened to come in a pleasing shape. I now think of the shape as one of the statements. A translation can fail by distorting the sense, but it can also fail by keeping the sense and discarding what the sense was doing.

In practice this has meant compromise, and compromise in translation is never comfortable. In my second book, I used rhyme where the poems seemed to depend on it and let it go where they did not. Sometimes I used near-rhymes—"stone" and "gone," "field" and "held"—which English readers hear as an echo rather than a chime. Sometimes I moved a rhyme from the end of a line to the middle, so that the collision still happened, if a little earlier. Purists on both sides have objected. Those who value accuracy say I have taken liberties; those who value form say I have not taken enough.

They are both right, and I have stopped expecting to satisfy either. A translation is a set of losses chosen on purpose. The translator's job is not to avoid loss—that is impossible—but to decide which losses the poem can survive. I did not know how to make that decision when I began. I learned it, in part, from a woman who had never translated anything, and who knew the poems better than I did because she had heard them before she could read.

candidates.subskill: Central idea of an argumentative essay
candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Rhymed translations of poetry are usually less accurate and less readable than unrhymed translations.
choices.B: Readers generally prefer translations that sound like poems to translations that are accurate.
choices.C: The author came to see a poem's form as part of its meaning and changed how the author translates.
choices.D: Readers who know a poem in its original language are the best judges of a translation's accuracy.

candidates.evidence: I now think of the shape as one of the statements.
candidates.explanation: The passage traces the author's change from treating rhyme as an accident to treating a poem's shape as 'one of the statements,' which led to the compromises of the second book.

A.rationale: This was the author's early view, which the passage describes the author revising.

B.rationale: One reader's letter prompts the change, but the passage makes no claim about what readers generally prefer.

D.rationale: The reader praised the versions as accurate; her objection was that they did not capture what the poems were like.

hints: How does the author's view at the end differ from the view at the start?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the change the author describes.

candidates.remember: In an essay about a change of mind, the main idea is usually the new position.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of the second paragraph is to:

choices.A: explain the reasoning behind a position the author later revised.
choices.B: argue that rhymed translations of poetry should no longer be published.
choices.C: describe the methods the author used to translate the second book.
choices.D: show that the author's first book was praised for its accuracy.

candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 lays out why the author once preferred unrhymed translation ('My reasoning seemed sound'); the rest of the passage shows that view changing.

B.rationale: The author distrusted such translations but makes no argument about publishing them.

C.rationale: The second book is described in paragraph 6.

D.rationale: Paragraph 2 describes the author's own pride, not anyone's praise; the reviews come in paragraph 3.

hints: Does the author still hold the view in paragraph 2?

strategy.explanation: Ask how the paragraph fits the whole essay.

candidates.remember: 'Seemed' signals a view the writer no longer fully holds.

candidates.stem: The reader's statement "You have not told me what they are like" (paragraph 3) most nearly means that the author's translations:

choices.A: contained mistakes that changed what the poems were about.
choices.B: were too difficult for most readers to follow and understand.
choices.C: should have been set to music, as the originals were.
choices.D: captured the poems' content but not how they felt to a listener.

candidates.evidence: You have told me what the poems say
candidates.explanation: She contrasts what the poems 'say' (which the versions captured accurately) with what they are 'like': their sound and feel, which were lost.

A.rationale: She calls the versions accurate, so mistakes in meaning are not her complaint.

B.rationale: Difficulty is never mentioned; the issue is what was missing.

C.rationale: The poems were sung to her, but she asks for their character, not a musical setting.

hints: What does she say the versions did get right?
candidates.remember: A contrast in a quotation often defines its meaning.

candidates.stem: According to paragraph 4, what had the author's accurate versions lost?

choices.A: The tension when similar-sounding words had opposing meanings
choices.B: One of the two words in each pair of rhyming words
choices.C: The regular rhythm and meter of the original lines
choices.D: The adjectives that rhymed translations add to fill out a line

candidates.evidence: My accurate versions had kept both words and lost the collision between them.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains that a rhyme word was answered by a similar-sounding word with a nearly opposite meaning, 'so that the ear heard agreement while the mind heard argument.' The unrhymed versions kept both words but lost that collision.

B.rationale: The author says the versions 'had kept both words.'

C.rationale: Rhythm is not discussed in paragraph 4.

D.rationale: Padding is what the author disliked in rhymed translations, not something the unrhymed versions lost.

hints: What did the versions keep, and what did they lose?

strategy.explanation: Read the last sentence of paragraph 4 closely.

candidates.remember: Read 'kept' and 'lost' in the same sentence carefully; traps reverse them.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 6, the word "chime" most nearly refers to:
candidates.evidence: which English readers hear as an echo rather than a chime
candidates.explanation: Near-rhymes such as 'stone' and 'gone' are heard 'as an echo rather than a chime,' so a chime is a full, exact rhyme, in contrast to the partial match of an echo.

A.rationale: This is the literal meaning; here the word describes how rhyming words sound together.

C.rationale: Paragraph 4 says the ear 'heard agreement,' but in paragraph 6 'chime' is contrasted with a looser 'echo.'

D.rationale: The contrast is between an exact and an approximate rhyme, not about melody.

hints: What is a chime contrasted with?

strategy.explanation: Use the contrast with 'echo' and the near-rhyme examples.

candidates.remember: A word contrasted with another often takes its meaning from that contrast.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 5, the author's description of a poem as "a set of statements that happened to come in a pleasing shape" suggests that the author had once regarded a poem's form as:

choices.A: the feature of a poem that matters most to its readers.
choices.B: something that no translator could reproduce in another language.
choices.C: an attractive feature that was not essential to the poem.
choices.D: a feature readers valued more highly than the poem's meaning.

candidates.evidence: I had treated a poem as a set of statements that happened to come in a pleasing shape.
candidates.explanation: 'Happened to come in a pleasing shape' presents form as an attractive accident laid over the real content, the statements. The next sentence ('I now think of the shape as one of the statements') confirms the author once thought form inessential.

A.rationale: This overstates even the author's later view, which treats form as one statement among others.

B.rationale: The author says rhyme is language-specific but never says form cannot be reproduced; the second book reproduces some of it.

D.rationale: The earlier view concerns what the author thought, not what readers valued.

hints: What does 'happened to' suggest about the shape?

strategy.explanation: Contrast the earlier and later descriptions of shape.

candidates.remember: Words like 'happened to' mark something as accidental.

candidates.subskill: Purpose of a technique described in the passage
candidates.stem: Based on the passage, the author most likely uses near-rhymes and moves rhymes to the middle of a line (paragraph 6) in order to:

choices.A: make the translations easier to sing, as the original poems were sung.
choices.B: satisfy the readers who value strict poetic form above accuracy.
choices.C: reproduce the rhyme schemes of the original poems exactly.
choices.D: keep a rhyme's effect while avoiding the distortion strict rhyme causes.

candidates.evidence: so that the collision still happened, if a little earlier
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 objects that strict rhyme forces padding and twisted lines; paragraph 4 values the 'collision' of sound and sense. Near-rhymes and moved rhymes keep the collision 'still happened' without forcing exact rhymes at line ends.

A.rationale: Nothing suggests the author is adapting the poems for singing.

B.rationale: Those readers object that the author 'has not taken enough' liberties.

C.rationale: Moving a rhyme to the middle of a line changes the scheme on purpose.

hints: What problem with strict rhyme did paragraph 2 describe?
candidates.remember: A compromise usually keeps part of each side's goal.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 7, the author's statement that the purists on both sides "are both right" most strongly suggests that the author:

choices.A: plans to return to unrhymed translation in future books.
choices.B: accepts that the compromise gives up some accuracy and some form.
choices.C: believes the two groups of purists secretly agree with each other.
choices.D: thinks most criticism of translators is unfair.

candidates.evidence: A translation is a set of losses chosen on purpose.
candidates.explanation: Each group objects to a different loss: accuracy (liberties taken) or form (not enough taken). Saying both are right admits both losses, which the author defends as 'losses chosen on purpose.'

A.rationale: Nothing suggests the author will abandon the compromise.

C.rationale: The two groups make opposite objections.

D.rationale: The author agrees with the criticism, calling both sides right.

hints: What does each group of purists complain about?

strategy.explanation: Read the objections at the end of paragraph 6.

candidates.remember: Agreeing with two opposed critics means admitting two kinds of cost.

candidates.subskill: Comparing a narrator’s views over time
candidates.stem: Which of the following beliefs does the author hold both at the beginning of the passage and at the end?

choices.A: A translation should follow each line of the original as closely as possible.
choices.B: A poem's shape is one of the things the poem says.
choices.C: Accuracy is the only fair standard for judging a translation.
choices.D: Forcing rhymes onto a translation can fill it with padding.

candidates.evidence: Some of the strictly rhymed translations I had distrusted really are as bad as I thought.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 objects to the padding forced rhyme creates, and paragraph 5 says some strictly rhymed translations 'really are as bad as I thought,' so this belief survives the change. The other choices are held only early or only late.

A.rationale: This is the early view behind the first book; the second book moved rhymes and used near-rhymes.

B.rationale: This is the author's later view, reached after the letter.

C.rationale: The author later says a translation can fail 'by keeping the sense and discarding what the sense was doing.'

hints: Which early opinion does paragraph 5 repeat?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against both the early and the later paragraphs.

candidates.remember: A lasting belief must be supported by both early and late paragraphs.

revision_log.reason: Round-1 blind solves (both matched every key) flagged that R033-06's key ('still critical of many' strictly rhymed translations) gave away R033-09's answer, and that R033-04 and R033-05 both turned on the same 'collision' sentence; several distractors were weak. Replaced 06 with an inference about the author's earlier view of form ('a pleasing shape'), replaced 05 with a vocabulary item on 'chime' (paragraph 6), and replaced an extreme distractor in 01. Passage unchanged. Whole batch re-solved blind.
